abstract: Summary Background Functional CAR-T cell exhaustion in the immunosuppressive tumour microenvironment remains the main barrier to the success of CAR-T cell therapy for treating solid tumours. Mesothelin (MSLN) has emerged as an attractive target for CAR-T cell therapy for several solid malignancies, including ovarian cancer. In this study, we aimed to investigate the role and mechanism of lipid metabolites in anti-MSLN CAR-T cell exhaustion in ovarian cancer cells. Methods We engineered anti-MSLN CAR-T cells targeting ovarian cancer cells with high MSLN expression as a pivotal tool for in vitro and in vivo experiments. Moreover, liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) revealed the critical role of oxylipin 12-HETE in the exhaustion of CAR-T cells. By employing structure-based high-throughput virtual screening (HTVS), we identified the inhibitor targeting B7-H3. Findings We demonstrated that GPR31-dependent 12-HETE accumulation in the ovarian cancer microenvironment drives CAR-T cell exhaustion via lipid peroxidation, impairing their antitumour efficacy. Genetic or pharmacological inhibition of the 12-HETE/GPR31 axis restored CAR-T cell cytotoxicity and proliferation, leading to significant tumour regression in murine models. Silencing B7-H3 relieved repression of FOXO3, leading to reduced 12-LOX expression and lower 12-HETE levels, which places B7-H3 upstream of this metabolic checkpoint. Through structure-based screening, we identified HI-TOPK-032 as a potent B7-H3 inhibitor that synergised with CAR-T cell therapy by reversing exhaustion markers (e.g., PD-1, TIM-3) and enhancing cytokine polyfunctionality. Combined HI-TOPK-032 and anti-PD-1 treatment achieved superior tumour control compared to monotherapies, particularly in B7-H3/12-LOX-high patient-derived xenografts, underscoring its precision therapeutic potential. Interpretation CAR-T cell therapy combined with HI-TOPK-032 is a promising novel strategy for treating MSLN-expressing solid tumours. Research in context
Evidence before this study
CAR-T cell therapy has shown significant efficacy in treating haematologic malignancies. However, translating these successes into solid tumour treatment poses considerable challenges, primarily due to CAR-T cell exhaustion within the immunosuppressive tumour microenvironment. Metabolic alterations and immunosuppressive cytokines within the tumour immune microenvironment are considered key factors contributing to CAR-T cells’ functional exhaustion.
Added value of this study
Here, we identify 12-HETE, a tumour-derived oxidised lipid, as a key mediator of CAR-T exhaustion via GPR31-dependent lipid peroxidation—a previously unrecognised metabolic checkpoint. Silencing B7-H3 relieved repression of FOXO3, leading to reduced 12-LOX expression and lower 12-HETE levels, which places B7-H3 upstream of this metabolic checkpoint. Through high-throughput virtual screening, we developed HI-TOPK-032, a first-in-class B7-H3 inhibitor that reduces 12-HETE production and restores CAR-T cytotoxicity. Crucially, HI-TOPK-032 synergises with CAR-T therapy to enhance tumour control not only in syngeneic models but also in B7-H3/12-LOX-high patient-derived xenografts, demonstrating translational relevance.
Implications of all the available evidence
This study provides new insights into the cross-talk between tumour and CAR-T cells via a mechanism of metabolite interaction. These findings suggest that HI-TOPK-032 can be used as an alternative synergetic agent with CAR-T cell therapy for clinical cancer treatment.
Introduction
Since the first clinical application of CD19-targeted chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T cell therapy for treating B-cell malignancies, substantial progress has been made in CAR-T cell therapy.
1
,
2
To date, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and the European Medicines Agency (EMA) have approved four different CAR-T cell constructs for treating CD19
+
haematologic malignancies.
3
,
4
,
5
,
6
Despite improvements in the CAR design, successful clinical responses to CAR-T cell therapy in solid tumours have not been achieved.
7
,
8
One of the current challenges in CAR-T cell therapy is how to avoid CAR-T cell exhaustion in different immunosuppressive tumour microenvironments (TMEs).
9
Metabolic changes within tumours and immunosuppressive cytokines are important factors leading to the loss of effector function in non-exhausted CAR-T cells.
10
Ovarian cancer displays a unique clinical feature termed “lipophilia”, a phenomenon in which cancer cells invade adipose-rich tissues in cases of advanced or recurrent disease.
11
Lipids can be transferred directly from adipocytes to ovarian cancer cells, and increased lipolysis of β-oxylipins in tumour cells can provide energy for tumour cell growth and metastasis.
12
,
13
Importantly, abnormal fatty acid oxidation metabolism in tumour cells leads to the accumulation of its byproduct oxylipins in the TME.
14
,
15
This phenomenon raises the following questions: Does the accumulation of oxylipins facilitate CAR-T cell rejection, potentially leading to CAR-T cell exhaustion? Can the inhibition of fatty acid oxidation in ovarian cancer cells restore CAR-T cell function? These questions have not yet been answered in ovarian cancer research.
Moving beyond the restricted expression of CD19 on the B-cell lineage and nearly uniform expression on B-cell malignancies, identifying ubiquitously expressed tumour-associated antigens in solid tumours with limited ‘on-target/off-tumour’ risk has proven complicated. Mesothelin (MSLN) is a surface protein with limited basal expression in nonmalignant tissues but is highly expressed in many malignant tumours, including ovarian cancer, malignant mesothelioma, and pancreatic cancer.
16
,
17
Promising results have been reported using MSLN-directed CAR-T cells in preclinical models,
18
and a recent phase I clinical trial demonstrated the safety of targeting MSLN as a CAR-T cell therapy antigen in late-stage solid cancer patients.
19
To successfully translate CAR-T cell therapy to solid tumours, researchers must elucidate the mechanisms affecting CAR-T cell exhaustion.
In this study, for the first time, we investigated the role of lipid metabolism, specifically the accumulation of oxylipins, in CAR-T cell exhaustion in tumours. We compared the exhaustion status of MSLN-CAR-T cells in different co-culture models. Ovarian cancer cell metabolites can promote CAR-T cell depletion. The level of oxidised lipids in ovarian cancer was significantly increased, and the level of the oxidised lipid 12-HETE was significantly increased. Ovarian cancer cells can release 12-HETE, promoting CAR-T cell depletion. 12-HETE promoted T-cell lipid peroxidation through GPR31, and inhibiting T-cell lipid peroxidation restored T-cell function. The mechanism of 12-HETE release in ovarian cancer cells was further explored. Inhibition of 12-HETE accumulation by the small-molecule compound HI-TOPK-032 promoted the antitumour effect of CAR-T cells. In addition, HI-TOPK-032 combined with an anti-PD-1 antibody inhibited CAR-T cell depletion and increased the immunotherapy efficacy.

We hypothesised that 12-HETE secreted by tumour cells is associated with CAR-T cell exhaustion. To test this hypothesis, first, we added 0, 0.5, 1, or 1.5 μM 12-HETE to the CAR-T cell medium. We found that 12-HETE dose-dependently inhibited the expression of cytokines at both the mRNA and protein levels (
Fig. 3
A–C,
Figure S8A–B
). Second, we observed more specific inhibition of 12-HETE production in the SKOV3-ML and OVCAR3-ML cells treated with CAY10698, a selective inhibitor of 12-lipoxygenase (12-LOX), which is known to inhibit the enzymatic activity of 12-LOX and subsequently reduce the production of 12-HETE.
25

Figure S9A–B

Fig. 3
D and
Figure S10A–E
). Finally, SKOV3-ML or OVCAR3-ML cells transiently overexpressing 12-LOX were used because of their high 12-HETE production upon arachidonic acid (AA) addition. In tumour cells, 12-HETE production increased at least 4-fold and was maintained at this level for 3 days after AA treatment (
Figure S9C–D
). As expected, tumour cells overexpressing 12-LOX were collected in culture medium after 24 h and cocultured with T cells, revealing a decrease in the secretion of IL-2 and GzmB by CAR-T cells and a decrease in Ki67 expression (
Fig. 3
D,
Figure S10A–E
). Taken together, these data suggest that tumour-derived 12-HETE promotes CAR-T cell exhaustion and inhibition of 12-HETE reverses CAR-T cell exhaustion.

Discussion
Currently, many ongoing clinical trials investigate MSLN-CAR-T-cell trials covering several malignancies, including malignant pleural mesothelioma, pancreatic cancer, lung cancer, and ovarian cancer, are ongoing. Safety profiles in clinical trials using MSLN-CAR-T cells have been favourable, with no overt clinical evidence of on-target/off-tumour toxicity. Despite promising results in preclinical models, the clinical response rates of MSLN-CAR-T cells have thus far been marginal, with limited persistence in the majority of patients.
2
The factors that contribute to poor efficacy can be summarised into two major categories: insufficient infiltration of CAR-T cells and exhaustion of CAR-T cells.
9
Here, we demonstrated that CAR-T-cell depletion is closely related to the TME.
In vivo
, the proliferative capacity (Ki-67) and killing potential (IFN-γ and TNF-α) of CAR-T cells in tumour tissues were decreased compared with those in peripheral blood, and the expression of depletion-related protein (PD-1) was increased (
Fig. 1
,
Figure S2
). This finding supports the view that the immunosuppressed tumour microenvironment severely limits the antitumour function of functional CAR-T cells.
40
Previous coculture experiments have shown that T-cell metabolism is influenced by other cell metabolites in the coculture medium.
41
,
42
,
43
Their findings suggest that changes in the secretory group (including TNF-α, glutamine, formate, and glutamate) in CM from coculture tests reflect different cytotoxicity outcomes for CAR-T cells.
44
,
45
,
46
Consistent with previous reports, we generated
in vitro
models in which coculture with tumour cells and their metabolites promoted CAR-T cell depletion. In addition, we highlighted the importance of antigen, as only coculture with MSLN-positive tumour cells inhibited CAR-T cell proliferation (
Fig. 1
,
Figure S3
).
CAR-T cells encounter multiple inhibitory mechanisms that may be affected by histological subtypes and previous antitumour therapies.
10
,
47
In addition to the intrinsic inhibitory mechanisms of T cells exemplified by the expression of immune checkpoint molecules on their surface (e.g., PD-1), anti-MSLN CAR-T cells are also affected by extrinsic suppressive features of the TME. These include the soluble mediators TGF-β and prostaglandin E (PGE2), which are produced mostly by immunosuppressive M2 tumour-associated macrophages (TAMs) and regulatory T cells (Tregs),
48
,
49
as well as adenosine, which is found at high levels as a result of hypoxia and the expression of the ectoenzymes CD39 and CD73.
50
In this study, we first assessed the unique TME of HGSOC; we confirmed by tissue staining and intracellular lipid peroxidation analysis that oxylipins are abundant in ovarian cancer TME (
Fig. 2
). Deregulated lipid metabolism is a hallmark of the TME, and increased lipid uptake and accumulation are observed in many types of intratumoral immune cells and are often associated with impaired antitumour immune function.
22
,
51
Using LC-MS/MS screening, we identified the critical role of oxylipin 12-HETE in the survival of CAR-T cells. 12-HETE, a product of fatty acid metabolism, is known for its roles in oxidative stress, inflammation, and cancer biology.
23
Our experiments demonstrated that 12-HETE, which is produced and secreted by ovarian cancer cells, promotes the exhaustion of CAR-T cells. Notably, these findings support the idea that 12-HETE plays an important role in the biological behaviour of malignant tumours, which has been discovered in recent years.
22
,
23
,
24
Two 12-HETE-binding receptors, GPR31 and LTB4R2, have been identified. Among them, GPR31, a high-affinity receptor for 12-HETE, can participate in T-cell development.
31
Previous studies have shown that the effect of 12-HETE on a hepatic ischaemia-reperfusion injury model is mediated by GPR31.
52
Multiple studies have shown that GPR31 plays a role in a variety of diseases, such as Alzheimer's disease, cardiovascular disease, and diabetic complications, by receiving signals from 12-HETE.
53
However, whether both receptors are associated with tumour-depleted CD8
+
T cells is unknown. Our results suggest that 12-HETE may promote CD8
+
T-cell depletion via GPR31. While further investigating the effects of GPR31 on T-cell dynamics, we became interested in lipid peroxidation in cancer. Lipid peroxidation refers to the oxidative deterioration of polyunsaturated fatty acids and lipids to form lipid peroxidation products such as malondialdehyde and 4-hydroxynonenoic acid. Lipid peroxidation can cause serious damage to the cell membrane, lipoproteins, and other lipid-containing structures, such as by changing the fluidity and permeability of the cell membrane and damaging proteins, thus affecting the normal function of cells. We examined the relationships among 12-HETE, the GPR31 receptor, and lipid peroxidation in CAR-T cells and observed that 12-HETE increased lipid peroxidation levels in CAR-T cells. The lipid peroxidation level of CAR-T cells decreased after si-GPR31 treatment. The lipid peroxidation of mouse GPR31
−/−
CD8
+
TILs was lower than that of GPR31
WT
CD8
+
TILs. The addition of antioxidants reversed the inhibitory effect of 12-HETE on the killing potential of CAR-T cells. This finding suggests that targeting lipid peroxidation may be a new direction for alleviating CAR-T-cell depletion in ovarian cancer.
Considering the critical role of GPR31 in T-cell growth and glucose metabolism, we aimed to “unbind” CAR-T cells by reducing the accumulation of 12-HETE through the regulation of ovarian cancer cells. Similar to previous results, we also found that 12-LOX was highly expressed in ovarian cancer and that the inhibition of 12-LOX prevented 12-HETE production. The activity of 12-LOX and the production of 12-HETE are associated with subclinical inflammation in pathological conditions such as diabetes mellitus, and the use of its inhibitor ML355 can regulate 12-LOX and subsequently regulate the NF-κB pathway, affecting cytokine proliferation. However, serious side effects of 12-LOX inhibitors have been reported in animals.
54
This finding suggests that the safety of current 12-LOX inhibitors still faces major challenges. Since 12-LOX is involved in various important metabolic processes in a variety of cells, it cannot be systemically blocked. The abnormally high expression of 12-LOX in ovarian cancer cells is triggered by abnormally activated molecules upstream, so alteration of the abnormal increase in 12-LOX can only be achieved by regulating upstream activated molecules. Moreover, 12-LOX is located inside the cell, so developing an antibody against 12-LOX will have difficulty crossing the cell membrane, resulting in no direct binding to 12-LOX to inhibit its activity. Using a small-range siRNA screening technique, we found that B7-H3 regulates the expression of 12-LOX. B7-H3 is a type I transmembrane protein. Recent studies and our experiments have shown that it is expressed not only in the cell membrane but also in the cytoplasm in large quantities.
35
The function of B7-H3 is far from limited to the field of immune response, and its multiple effects on driving metabolic reprogramming are equally important.
55
Most studies have focused on the regulatory effect of B7-H3 on glucose metabolism, and our study revealed for the first time that B7-H3 can promote the expression of 12-LOX and the secretion of 12-HETE. This finding suggested that B7-H3 also plays an important role in lipid metabolism in tumours. Future work should include targeted
in vitro
assays—such as co-cultures with B7-H3–deficient vs. –sufficient tumour cells or reporter assays for downstream pathways—to more directly probe B7-H3's signalling functions.
A monoclonal antibody against B7-H3 increased the activity of CD8
+
T cells and NK cells in animal models of ovarian cancer and melanoma and prolonged survival.
56
,
57
However, B7-H3 is a transmembrane protein, and the antibody can bind only to the extracellular Fc segment and cannot inhibit the function of its intracellular region or the region that has been expressed in the cytoplasm. Therefore, the clinical application of these methods is limited. There is an urgent need to find a substance that can fundamentally eliminate the full effect of B7-H3. Small molecule drugs, which can efficiently and selectively kill tumour cells and reduce damage to normal tissues, have unique targeted antitumour effects and play important roles in the clinical treatment of various malignant tumours, such as lymphoma, skin cancer, and soft tissue sarcoma. Moreover, no inhibitor of B7-H3 has been found. In this study, the small molecule compound HI-TOPK-032
39
was screened through a structure-based drug screening platform, and we showed that this molecule inhibited the expression of the B7-H3 protein and had inhibitory effects on both 12-LOX and 12-HETE. In addition, the small molecule compound HI-TOPK-032 inhibited the expression of B7-H3, inhibited the accumulation of 12-HETE, and promoted the antitumour effect of CAR-T cells. HI-TOPK-032 combined with an anti-PD-1 antibody inhibited CAR-T-cell depletion and increased the immunotherapy efficacy. Although our study focused on the combination of HI-TOPK-032 with B7-H3-targeted CAR-T cells, the modulation of the tumour microenvironment observed here may not be antigen-specific. Given the common challenges of T cell dysfunction and immunosuppression across different solid tumours, it is possible that HI-TOPK-032 could similarly enhance the activity of CAR-T cells targeting other tumour-associated antigens.
Our study population was exclusively Han Chinese from a single institution. While this homogeneity enhances the internal validity of our findings by minimising genetic and socioeconomic confounding, it may limit the generalisability of our results to other ethnic and healthcare settings.
In conclusion, we show that elevated 12-HETE in the ovarian tumour microenvironment drives CAR-T cell exhaustion through GPR31-mediated lipid peroxidation. Silencing B7-H3 relieved repression of FOXO3, leading to reduced 12-LOX expression and lower 12-HETE levels, which places B7-H3 upstream of this metabolic checkpoint. Consistently, HI-TOPK-032–mediated inhibition of B7-H3 decreased 12-HETE production and restored CAR-T cell cytotoxicity
in vivo
. When combined with anti–PD-1 therapy, this approach yielded the most pronounced tumour regression, underscoring the therapeutic promise of targeting the B7-H3/12-HETE/GPR31 axis.
Limitations of the study
Although our study provides important insights into the interplay of B7-H3, oxylipins, and immune responses in ovarian cancer, certain limitations warrant consideration. Our findings regarding the 12-HETE-mediated suppression of CAR-T cell infiltration provide a possible mechanism for immune intervention; however, the intricate network of factors contributing to immune evasion in the ovarian cancer microenvironment may involve additional unexplored mechanisms. The impact of 12-HETE on other immune cell populations remains to be fully elucidated in our future study. Unfortunately, due to the lack of a resolved crystal or high-resolution structure for B7-H3, it is challenging to identify and discuss specific amino acid sequences that play important roles in its structure. While our study introduces a potential small molecule compound, HI-TOPK-032, as a means to modulate B7-H3 expression and promote immune responses, challenges remain in translating this approach to clinical applications. The absence of conclusive evidence for a direct binding interaction is a noteworthy limitation. The compound's safety, specificity, and effectiveness in diverse patient populations, as well as its potential off-target effects, necessitate thorough preclinical and clinical assessments. Due to small tumour size and all samples being used for single-cell suspension flow cytometry, we did not investigate CAR-T cell distribution by IHC. The limited sample sizes in animal experiments may reduce the power to detect smaller effects and should be considered when interpreting the results. Additionally, the results from ID-8 cell-implanted mice may not fully translate to human ovarian cancer due to differences in tumour biology and the immune microenvironment. We acknowledge that all patient samples were collected from a single centre, which may limit the generalisability of the findings; further validation in multi-centre cohorts will be valuable. In summary, while our study provides innovative insights into the immune landscape of ovarian cancer, it is important to acknowledge the complexities of the TME and the need for continued investigation into these mechanisms. Addressing these limitations will contribute to the development of more effective and targeted therapies for ovarian cancer immunotherapy.
